extracted.intended_audience: small law firms and SMMEs (small, medium and micro enterprises) in South Africa
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and checklists for commercialising, managing, protecting and enforcing intellectual property rights (IPRs) for small law firms and SMMEs in South Africa, including licensing, assignment, valuation, audits, budgeting and strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: IP commercialisation definition & influencing factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of bringing the IPRs to market for them to be exploited in return for business profits and growth. The way the IPRs are exploited will depend on internal and external factors including market factors, the relevant industry, business structure and objective, business culture, strategy, resources available, and the nature of the IPRs concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Businesses may use IPRs internally, assign/sell them, or license/franchise/joint venture. Choose exploitation route based on those internal/external factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align IP protection with business and marketing strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Protection of your IPRs should be aligned with the business and marketing strategy of your company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider future growth, expansion into other regions/countries and online channels when planning protection. If a trade mark is adapted or evolves in use, consider whether a new trade mark should be filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper record keeping and evidence of use
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain proper records of the creation and use of IPRs to support evidence such as acquired goodwill through use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document creation dates, use in commerce, sales, marketing, and maintain archives that can support enforcement and valuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review contractual provisions (employment & third-party)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review agreements and contracts used within the business (employment, third-party) to ensure they include appropriate IP provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreements should cover confidentiality clauses, ownership and title to IPRs created during employment or commissioned work, technical testing, and required disclosures. Ensure clarity on who owns IP and required assignments or licenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include alternative dispute resolution clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider including alternative dispute resolution (ADR) clauses in contracts to address potential conflicts efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ADR clauses can reduce litigation costs and time; include them in employment, licensing, assignment and service agreements where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor market and competitors for infringements
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuously monitor the market and competitors to identify possible infringements of your IPRs so as to take quick and proactive action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make monitoring part of IP management processes; assign responsibility and set reporting intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement responsibility lies with the IPR owner
rubrics_metrics.description: The enforcement of the IPRs is the responsibility of the IPR owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners must be prepared and budgeted to enforce rights; external counsel or enforcement partners can be engaged when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure supply chain and implement IP policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Secure your supply chain and adopt and implement policies and procedures to manage the use and protection of IPRs in the supply chain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include contractual IP protections with suppliers and distributors, traceability, and compliance monitoring to mitigate leakage or unauthorised use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment must be written, recorded and specific
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment (sale/transfer) is a written contract where an IPR owner sells the rights and title to another party. Any assignment agreement must be recorded in the relevant registry against the registered IPR to be valid against third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before assigning, ensure NDAs in place, check IPR status (registered vs pending), assess restrictions on future trading, and ensure the assignment is in writing specifying parties, the IPRs, payment terms, warranties, governing law, effective date and signatures. If not recorded in the registry, assignment may only be valid between the parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use NDAs before negotiations
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) are in place before entering negotiations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NDAs protect confidential information disclosed during negotiations and should be used before sharing sensitive IP or business information in sale, licensing, franchising or partnership talks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check IPR status before assignment or licensing
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the IPR is pending or registered before assigning or licensing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only a registered trade mark can be assigned in the registry; for pending applications a substitution of applicant may be recorded. Check registry requirements for recordal of licenses/assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess restrictions on future trade when transferring IP
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the sale or licensing of the IPR will have any restrictions on your future ability to trade or carry on business in relation to the goods or services covered by the IPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how assignment/licensing affects business operations and competition; include appropriate covenants or carve-outs in agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of licence and selecting appropriate type
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose licence type based on business objectives and nature of goods/services: Exclusive, Sole, or Non-exclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusive: only the licensee can use the right (licensor cannot use or license further). Sole: licensor agrees not to grant further licences but retains the right to use. Non-exclusive: both licensor and licensee can use the right and licensor can license others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written, signed licence agreement with key terms
rubrics_metrics.description: A licence agreement should be in writing and signed; it must clearly outline parties, the licensed IPRs, terms and conditions, payment details, warranties, governing laws, and the effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For patents and designs, the agreement should also address treatment of future improvements. Check specific registry recordal requirements for licenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider costs of securing and enforcing IPRs when valuing or pricing
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining purchase price or valuation consider the costs of securing and enforcing the IPRs, in addition to profits and potential market value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include anticipated enforcement costs, prosecution, renewals, foreign filings and possible infringement litigation in pricing and valuation assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Franchising requires specialist advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Franchising is a form of licence with obligations on franchisor to maintain training/know-how; the franchise agreement is complex and franchisors should seek professional advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to Franchise Association of South Africa (FASA) and consider mediation/complaints processes. Franchising involves coordinated marketing and developed business systems — legal and commercial advice is urged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exchange control approvals for offshore transfer of IP
rubrics_metrics.description: The transfer of South African owned IPRs offshore is subject to South African Exchange Control Regulations; export of capital or right to capital (including IPR) requires permission from Exchange Control Authorities of the Reserve Bank (SARB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All exchange control matters must be addressed through an Authorised Dealer (registered bank or authorised dealer in foreign exchange). Failure to comply may be a criminal offence punishable by fine and/or imprisonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of tax implications of IPR transactions
rubrics_metrics.description: IPR owners need to be aware of tax implications related to development and creation of IPRs (R&D incentives, rebates, deduction of legal expenses), royalties (withholding tax), sale of IPRs (capital gains tax considerations), and VAT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider company structure and ownership of IPRs before deciding on business structure or whether IPRs should be held in a holding company; expert legal and tax advice is urged.

rubrics_metrics.name: IP valuation purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Valuation of IP determines monetary value of company IP assets for various reasons including financial transactions (M&A, royalties, license agreements), financial reporting/tax (impairment), legal (damages for infringement), and other strategic objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify purpose before selecting valuation method; use valuations to inform negotiation, tax reporting, litigation quantification, and strategic decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: IP valuation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Different methods adopted in determining IP value: income method (value based on income derived), market method (price of IPR transferred in similar circumstances), cost method (calculating cost of similar IP assets), relief-from-royalties method, and technology method (IP portfolio review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select method appropriate to valuation purpose; WIPO resources provide further guidance on methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate IP management with business strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: IP oversight should be integrated into the overall business strategy; IP strategy sets out how to develop, manage, protect and commercialise IP and aligns with business goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IP strategy is influenced by business stage, industry, competitors and resources. Use an IP strategy framework early to secure buy-in and early protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use external IP portfolio management when lacking internal expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: External IP portfolio management via an identified IP specialist/company is recommended for start-ups or developing businesses lacking internal specialist skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External partners can ensure formalities are met and provide industry knowledge, but businesses must maintain internal systems to track and manage IP even when outsourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign an IP manager or responsible function
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure responsibility for creation and management of the IP strategy is delegated to an individual or department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designate clear roles and reporting lines for IP tasks, renewals, monitoring and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality protections for sensitive IP
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure mechanisms exist to keep confidential information safe and limit exposure (employment contracts, NDAs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control access, use NDAs and confidentiality clauses, and limit the number of people exposed to sensitive information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the source of IP and ensure you own the IP; where ownership cannot be obtained, ensure a proper licence agreement exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify ownership when working with third parties, contractors or employees; have signed assignments or licences to avoid disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training staff and partners about IP
rubrics_metrics.description: Educate business partners and staff about IP, IPRs and their value, responsibilities and steps to safeguard IP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide regular training, induction materials and clear policies so staff understand confidentiality and invention disclosure processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: IP mapping: identify what to protect and how to use it
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide which parts of your goods or services you want to protect, identify the IP and determine how best to use the IP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform an IP mapping exercise to prioritise filings, budget and enforcement resources in line with business goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set IP objectives and protection measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Set out goals for IP strategy considering business plan objectives; identify IP and ensure it is properly protected and maintained through timely renewals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include IP goals in business planning and schedule renewals to avoid lapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider IP costs and budgeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider costs of securing protection (filing, examination, prosecution, registration, renewals) and maintenance of IPRs when budgeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request annual estimates from external IP partners, include a buffer (recommended 10-20%) for variances, and review IP costs quarterly alongside the business budget.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documenting IP processes and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Create processes for recording, saving and storing IP, including evidence of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain organised records for filings, licences, assignments, commercialization activities and evidence to support enforcement or valuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting requirements and intervals
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide on reporting requirements and intervals to ensure a proactive approach for new IP created.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish periodic reporting to management/board on IP status, renewals, budget, potential infringements and portfolio value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for growth and international protection needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider medium-term/long-term business strategy to identify future regions of importance and ensure IPRs are protected before entering new markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate expansion and file/maintain rights in jurisdictions that matter for market entry, supply chains and enforcement (including neighbouring territories and major ports).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct IP audits regularly
rubrics_metrics.description: IP audits are reviews of business IP, policies and agreements; they should be conducted at least once a year to identify assets, renewals, agreements and risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annual IP audits (and internal annual audits) help adapt strategy; request IP portfolio reports from external managers, capture deadlines/due dates, and record quarterly objectives for follow-up and timely action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use WIPO IP strategy staging
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow staged IP strategy framework: Stage 1 Ideation (generating/developing ideas); Stage 2 Product & Service Development (commercial and market analysis); Stage 3 IP Protection (securing assets); Stage 4 IP Commercialisation (market entry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use WIPO's step-by-step IP Strategy Checklist for SMEs to structure the strategy and prevent common start-up pitfalls.
